title: Unit 3: Work, Energy, and Power

topics.name: Potential energy and conservation of energy

guide.title: Work, energy, and power: review guide
guide.intro: Energy methods connect a system's starting and ending states without tracking every force moment by moment. In Physics C, work is an integral, force comes from potential energy as a derivative, and power is a rate.
guide.equationNote: g = 10 m/s² unless a question says otherwise.

sections.title: Work and the work–energy theorem
body: The work done by a force along a path is W = ∫F·dr; for a force along x, W = ∫F(x) dx, the area under the F–x graph. A constant force gives W = Fd cos θ.
Work–energy theorem: the net work done on an object equals its change in kinetic energy, W_net = ΔK = ½mv_f² − ½mv_i².
points: Only the component of a force along the displacement does work.
Work can be negative: friction usually removes kinetic energy.
A spring force F = −kx does work −½k(x_f² − x_i²).

sections.title: Potential energy and conservation of energy
body: For a conservative force, F = −dU/dx: the force points downhill on a graph of U(x). Conversely, ΔU = −∫F dx. Gravity near Earth gives U = mgh, and a spring gives U = ½kx².

Equilibrium points are where dU/dx = 0: stable at a minimum of U (d²U/dx² > 0) and unstable at a maximum. With only conservative forces, K + U stays constant; nonconservative forces such as friction change the mechanical energy by the work they do.
points: You can put the zero of potential energy anywhere; only changes matter.
Mechanical energy removed by friction becomes thermal energy, so the total energy is still conserved.

sections.title: Power
body: Power is the rate of doing work or transferring energy: P = dW/dt. A force F acting on an object moving at velocity v delivers P = Fv cos θ.
Over time, the work done is the integral of power, W = ∫P dt. Average power is W/Δt.
points: At constant speed against a resistive force, the engine's power equals the resistive force times the speed.
More power does the same work in less time.

example.prompt: A 2.0 kg block moves along the x-axis under a force F(x) = 12 − 4x newtons. It starts from rest at x = 0. How fast is it moving at x = 2.0 m?
example.solution: W = ∫₀² (12 − 4x) dx = [12x − 2x²]₀² = 24 − 8 = 16 J. By the work–energy theorem, ½(2.0)v² = 16 J, so v = 4.0 m/s.

misconceptions: That holds only for a constant force along the motion; otherwise integrate.
Only differences in U matter, so choose the zero for convenience.
“A force that does no work is not acting.”
A force perpendicular to the motion acts on the object but does no work.
“Power and energy are the same thing.”
Power is the rate at which energy is transferred.

questions.prompt: A force F(x) = 3x² newtons acts along the x-axis. How much work does it do as an object moves from x = 0 to x = 2.0 m?
choiceExplanations: 24 J treats the force as constant at its final value, F(2) = 12 N, over the 2.0 m.
12 is F(2), a force in newtons, not the work.
2.7 J integrates x² and drops the factor 3.

questions.prompt: A 2.0 kg object moving at 3.0 m/s has 20 J of net work done on it. What is its final speed?
choiceExplanations: 4.5 m/s = √20 ignores the object's starting kinetic energy of 9 J.
13 m/s adds 20 J ÷ 2.0 kg = 10 to the speed; work changes kinetic energy, not speed directly.
29 is v²; the square root is still needed.

questions.prompt: A conservative force has potential energy U(x) = 4x² joules, with x in meters. What is the force at x = 1.5 m?
questions.explanation: F = −dU/dx = −8x, so F(1.5) = −12 N. The force points toward x = 0, back down the potential-energy curve.
choiceExplanations: The minus sign in F = −dU/dx matters: the force points toward lower potential energy.
9.0 is U(1.5) = 4(1.5)², an energy in joules, not the force.
The derivative of 4x² is 8x, not 4x.

questions.prompt: A spring with k = 200 N/m is compressed 0.10 m and used to launch a 0.050 kg ball straight up. How high above its launch point does the ball rise? (g = 10 m/s², ignore air resistance)
questions.explanation: The spring's energy ½kx² = ½(200)(0.10)² = 1.0 J becomes gravitational energy mgh: h = 1.0 J ÷ (0.050 × 10 N) = 2.0 m.
choiceExplanations: 4.0 m uses kx² without the factor ½.
40 m uses kx/mg, the spring's force instead of its stored energy.
20 m divides the energy by the mass alone instead of by the weight, mg.

questions.prompt: An object moves in a potential U(x) = x³ − 3x (SI units). Where are its equilibrium points, and which is stable?
choices: x = 1 and x = −1; x = 1 is stable
x = 1 and x = −1; x = −1 is stable
x = 1 and x = −1; both are stable
questions.explanation: Equilibrium where dU/dx = 3x² − 3 = 0, so x = ±1. d²U/dx² = 6x is positive at x = 1 (a minimum of U: stable) and negative at x = −1 (a maximum: unstable).
choiceExplanations: x = −1 is a maximum of U; a small push sends the object away from it.
Only a minimum of U is stable; x = −1 is a maximum.
At x = 0, dU/dx = −3 ≠ 0, so a force acts there and it is not an equilibrium.

questions.prompt: A 2.0 kg block starts from rest at the top of a ramp 3.0 m high and slides to the bottom. Friction does −20 J of work on it. What is its speed at the bottom? (g = 10 m/s²)
questions.explanation: mgh + W_friction = ½mv²: 60 J − 20 J = 40 J, so ½(2.0)v² = 40 and v = √40 ≈ 6.3 m/s.
choiceExplanations: 7.7 m/s = √60 ignores the 20 J removed by friction.
4.5 m/s = √20 subtracts the friction work from the wrong energy: only 20 J of the 60 J is lost.
8.9 m/s = √80 adds the friction work instead of subtracting it.

questions.prompt: A motor lifts a 50 kg load 4.0 m at constant speed in 10 s. What is its average power output? (g = 10 m/s²)
choiceExplanations: 2000 is the work in joules; it still has to be divided by the time.
20 W uses the mass instead of the weight (mg).
20,000 W multiplies by the time instead of dividing.

questions.prompt: A car travels at a constant 30 m/s against a total resistive force of 1500 N. What power must the engine deliver?
questions.explanation: At constant speed the driving force equals the resistive force, so P = Fv = (1500 N)(30 m/s) = 45,000 W = 45 kW.
choiceExplanations: 50 is F/v; power is force times velocity.
22.5 kW includes a factor ½ that does not belong in P = Fv.

questions.prompt: The power delivered to an object is P(t) = 6t² watts. How much work is done on it from t = 0 to t = 2.0 s?
choiceExplanations: 48 J treats the power as constant at its final value, P(2) = 24 W, for 2.0 s.
24 is P(2), a power in watts, not the work done.
2.7 J integrates t² and drops the factor 6.
